lesson.title: Continuity From Just One Direction: Left- and Right-Continuity
lesson.summary: One-sided continuity asks whether a function matches its limit approaching from only the left or only the right, which is exactly the tool needed to handle endpoints and describe how a function behaves right at a break.
lesson.body:
A one-sided limit only looks at what happens as x approaches c from a single direction. Right-continuity at c means the function matches its incoming value from the right: lim(x to c+) f(x) = f(c). Left-continuity at c means the mirror statement: lim(x to c-) f(x) = f(c). These are weaker requirements than full, two-sided continuity, because each one only demands agreement along half of the approach.

The link back to ordinary continuity at a point is exact and useful: f is continuous at c if and only if f is both left-continuous and right-continuous at c. If the two one-sided limits exist but disagree with each other, or if one of them fails to match f(c) while the other succeeds, then f is continuous from at most one side, and two-sided continuity fails. This is precisely why continuity on a closed interval [a, b] only asks for right-continuity at a and left-continuity at b, since those are the only directions of approach that exist from inside the interval at an endpoint.

Worked example: let f(x) = floor(x), the greatest integer function, and examine x = 2. For x in [2, 3), floor(x) = 2, so f(2) = 2. Approaching from the right, lim(x to 2+) floor(x) = 2, which matches f(2), so f is right-continuous at 2. Approaching from the left, for x in [1, 2), floor(x) = 1, so lim(x to 2-) floor(x) = 1, which does not match f(2) = 2. So f is right-continuous at 2 but not left-continuous, and therefore not continuous at 2 in the ordinary two-sided sense. This right-continuous-but-not-left-continuous pattern repeats at every integer for the floor function.

A second example makes the opposite pattern concrete. Define f(x) = x^2 for x <= 1 and f(x) = 2x for x > 1. Here f(1) = 1^2 = 1. Approaching from the left, lim(x to 1-) f(x) = lim(x to 1-) x^2 = 1, which matches f(1), so f is left-continuous at 1. Approaching from the right, lim(x to 1+) f(x) = lim(x to 1+) 2x = 2, which does not match f(1) = 1. So this function is left-continuous but not right-continuous at x = 1, and overall discontinuous there, even though each piece is a perfectly smooth polynomial on its own side.

One-sided continuity is the precise language behind the endpoint condition from continuity on an interval, and it will also describe how jump discontinuities behave later: a function can be continuous from one side of a jump and simply fail from the other, rather than failing symmetrically. Recognizing which side, if either, still matches is often the fastest way to pin down exactly what kind of break a function has at a point, before working out the full classification of the discontinuity.

It also helps to notice what one-sided continuity does not claim. Being right-continuous at c says nothing about behavior to the left of c, and it certainly does not guarantee two-sided continuity there. A function can be right-continuous at every point of its domain, as the floor function is at every integer, and still fail to be continuous almost everywhere, since two-sided continuity is a strictly stronger statement than either one-sided version alone. Keeping the two ideas separate, one-sided continuity as a building block and two-sided continuity as the full requirement, avoids a common mix-up when reading endpoint conditions on closed intervals.
